title: [Dropbox Tech] Improving infrastructure efficiency for growing demand in the age of AI
summary: As demand for AI continues to grow, so does the infrastructure needed to support it. Much of the industry's attention has focused on building more: more data centers, more servers, and more power. But building new infrastructure is only part of the challenge. Engineering teams are also working within constraints on energy, cooling, hardware availability, and physical space, making it increasingly important to get more from the infrastructure that's already in place. For over a decade, Dropbox’s Infrastructure and Datacenter Engineering teams have continually improved how we plan, operate, and optimize infrastructure. That work spans far more than storage systems. Engineers across Dropbox work together on capacity planning, fleet optimization, hardware lifecycle management, power delivery, cooling, rack design, and facility planning. Rather than treating these as independent problems, we optimize them as parts of a single system, where decisions in one layer influence what's possible in another. The result is an engineering discipline that extends beyond any single system or optimization. A change in one part of the infrastructure can create opportunities or constraints elsewhere. Increasing storage density, for example, can reduce the amount of hardware needed, while more powerful servers can introduce new energy and cooling requirements. Understanding those tradeoffs allows us to make infrastructure decisions with the entire system in mind. As infrastructure demand grows, that system-level approach helps us prioritize efficiency and create room for growth before expanding our data center footprint. Planning for efficient infrastructure Many of the decisions that shape infrastructure efficiency happen months or sometimes years before new capacity goes into production. Whether someone is uploading a file to Dropbox or asking Dash a question, they expect the product to respond without delay. Delivering that experience requires engineers to forecast how customer demand and workloads will change, determine when additional resources will be needed, and understand whether our existing environments can support them. Dropbox has operated large-scale infrastructure for over a decade. Our hybrid model combines Magic Pocket, the core Dropbox storage system, with colocated data centers, where we manage our own servers and networking equipment in facilities operated by specialized providers. This gives our engineers visibility across software, hardware, and the physical data center environment. As customer demand grows and workloads change, particularly with the growth of AI-powered products and features, engineers have to plan not only for how much additional capacity is needed, but where and how it can be deployed. New hardware has to fit within a facility's infrastructure constraints while accounting for hardware availability and future product needs. A server that provides more compute or storage, for example, may also require more energy or cooling, changing how much hardware a rack or facility can support. The goal is to understand those tradeoffs early, add capacity deliberately, and preserve enough headroom for growth, maintenance, failures, and changing workloads. Once additional compute and storage capacity is deployed, the focus shifts to making the most of the systems already in production. Continuously optimizing the active fleet Planning helps ensure infrastructure is ready for anticipated demand, but workloads rarely behave exactly as they did when that infrastructure was first deployed. Customer behavior changes, products evolve, and new capabilities introduce different demands on the underlying systems. AI is a prime example because AI-powered features can change both the scale and shape of infrastructure demand, placing new demands on compute, storage, memory, and networking. That makes efficiency an ongoing engineering problem. Rather than treating deployed infrastructure as fixed, Dropbox continually adapts how the active fleet operates as those demands change. Sometimes that means reducing how much hardware is in use when demand is lower. Sometimes it means shifting work to parts of the fleet with resources available. And in other instances, advances in hardware allow the same physical infrastructure to support substantially more storage. These approaches work at different layers of the system, but they share the same objective: getting more useful capacity from the infrastructure already in place before adding more of it. Letting capacity rest when it isn't needed Infrastructure has to be provisioned for periods of higher demand, with additional headroom built in for reliability and maintenance. That means not all available capacity is needed at all times. When hardware is sitting idle or excess capacity is available, keeping every component fully powered consumes energy without providing additional value. Deep Sleep is one way Dropbox reduces that overhead. Deep Sleep is a Dropbox infrastructure initiative that reduces power consumption when hardware isn't actively needed. Depending on the hardware, that can mean spinning down hard drives into standby mode or powering down idle servers altogether. A server becomes eligible for Deep Sleep through automated fleet management algorithms. Dropbox is able to balance energy efficiency with performance and reliability because servers can return to service within minutes. For workloads that require lower latency, we can also selectively spin down idle hard drives rather than powering down the entire server. The challenge is determining where those power-saving measures can be applied safely. Engineers have to preserve enough available capacity to meet operational and reliability requirements while identifying hardware that doesn't need to remain fully powered. That allows Dropbox to reduce the energy consumed by underused infrastructure without compromising the capacity our products depend on. Reducing the power consumed by idle hardware is one way to make the existing fleet more efficient. Another is making better use of the infrastructure that's already online. Balancing work across the fleet Having enough capacity to meet overall demand is only part of operating infrastructure efficiently. That capacity also needs to be available where the work is happening. One part of the fleet may be approaching its limits while another has room to take on more work. Without a way to address that imbalance, Dropbox could end up adding more infrastructure instead of making better use of what’s already available across the fleet. To avoid that, Dropbox continually monitors how workloads are using resources across our infrastructure. The team identifies imbalances by monitoring spare capacity and workload distribution across the fleet, looking for areas where available headroom is falling or work is concentrating unevenly. When demand is uneven, teams can rebalance workloads across systems or bring additional capacity online where it's needed. Some adjustments happen automatically, while larger changes are reviewed and validated by engineers. This allows us to take advantage of available resources elsewhere rather than treating a localized constraint as a need for more infrastructure overall. That balancing has to continue as the fleet changes. Customer behavior shifts, products introduce new workload patterns, and the infrastructure itself evolves. Continually adapting where work runs helps Dropbox get more from the capacity that's already online. Balancing workloads helps make better use of the capacity we already have, but efficiency can also come from increasing how much that infrastructure can support in the first place. Increasing storage density Another way to get more from existing infrastructure is to increase how much each piece of hardware can support. Advances in storage technology have allowed Dropbox to store significantly more customer data on each drive. One example is shingled magnetic recording, which packs data more densely onto a hard drive without increasing its physical size. Those gains compound across the infrastructure. When each drive holds more data, fewer drives are needed to provide the same amount of storage. That can mean fewer servers and racks, less cabling, and lower power and cooling requirements. In turn, increasing the capacity of a single component can reduce the resources required across an entire deployment. That system-level impact is also why total power consumption doesn't tell the full story of efficiency. As Dropbox grows and stores more customer data, overall energy use may increase even as the infrastructure becomes more efficient. A more useful measure is watts per petabyte, or the amount of power required to support a petabyte of storage. Since 2020, watts per petabyte across our storage infrastructure have improved by more than 50%. Today, it takes less than half as much power to support the same amount of storage as it did in 2020. Together, all of the approaches described above help Dropbox get more from existing infrastructure by reducing unnecessary power consumption, making better use of available capacity and increasing how much each piece of hardware can support. How long that hardware can reliably remain in service matters, too. Extending infrastructure over time Replacing equipment too early can leave useful capacity on the table, while keeping it too long can introduce reliability and performance risks. Hardware doesn’t become unreliable simply because it reaches a particular age, nor does keeping equipment longer always make sense. To make those decisions, Dropbox monitors how hardware performs in production. Metrics such as annual failure rate help engineers understand how different components and generations of equipment behave over time. As demand for infrastructure continues to grow, those lifecycle decisions become increasingly important. Getting more from existing infrastructure isn't only about how efficiently hardware operates while it's in service. It's also about understanding how long that hardware can continue operating reliably before additional investment is needed. That data informs whether hardware can remain in service, should be repaired, or needs to be replaced. Understanding hardware performance holistically allows us to extend the useful life of equipment when it continues to perform reliably instead of relying solely on a fixed replacement schedule. When performance declines or newer hardware provides meaningful improvements in capacity, reliability, or efficiency, we can plan a transition. Reliability comes first. Extending a hardware lifecycle is valuable only when equipment continues to meet our operational standards. We repair hardware whenever practical to extend its useful life. When equipment can no longer remain in service at Dropbox, we work with trusted partners to resell or responsibly recycle it. Together, these decisions help maximize the value of equipment throughout its lifecycle rather than treating deployment and replacement as the only meaningful milestones. But eventually, new hardware does need to come online. And as servers become more powerful and storage becomes denser, deploying them can introduce a new set of constraints in the physical infrastructure that supports them. Engineering beyond the hardware Deploying new hardware isn't as simple as swapping one server for another. Before new hardware can go into production, the physical environment has to be able to support it. Our team plans for the power, airflow, rack layout, cabling, and other physical requirements each deployment needs, working closely with our colocation providers along the way. Those decisions are closely connected. A server that stores more data or delivers more compute may also draw more power or generate more heat. That can change how racks are designed, how equipment is cooled, and even how much hardware a particular area of a data center can support. As infrastructure becomes more powerful and denser, getting more from the hardware depends on making sure the environment around it can evolve, too. One recent example illustrates how those tradeoffs play out in practice. As Dropbox deployed its seventh-generation servers, the increased power requirements exceeded the capacity of the existing rack power design. Rather than rebuilding the underlying facility infrastructure, the Hardware Engineering and Datacenter Engineering teams redesigned the rack power architecture, doubling the number of power distribution units per rack while continuing to use the existing busways. The result supported the new hardware without requiring major changes to the data center itself. It's a reminder that infrastructure improvements don't stop with the hardware itself. As demand grows and hardware evolves to meet it, each new generation has to fit within the constraints of the environment around it. What years of operating infrastructure have taught us The work reflects more than a decade of engineering investment across Dropbox's infrastructure. Capacity planning, fleet optimization, storage systems, hardware lifecycle management, and data center engineering each address different challenges, but together they help us make better use of the infrastructure that supports our products. None of this work is one and done. As customer demands change, hardware evolves, and new technologies introduce opportunities and new constraints, we improve our infrastructure, each update building on the ones that came before it. Those lessons have become even more relevant as demand for digital infrastructure continues to grow. AI is accelerating the need for storage and compute across the industry, but the underlying engineering challenge hasn't changed. Infrastructure still has to scale while remaining reliable, efficient, and resilient. As these technologies evolve, we'll continue building systems that support the products our customers rely on today while giving us the flexibility to support what's next. ~ ~ ~ If building innovative products, experiences, and infrastructure excites you, come build the future with us! title: [Docker] AI Agent Security Risks: What Can Go Wrong When Agents Act on Their Own
summary: The thing that makes an AI agent useful, its freedom to act, is also what can introduce risk. An agent doesn’t just answer a question, it browses, runs code, and calls tools on its own, so a single bad or manipulated instruction can turn into real damage instead of just a wrong answer. That’s the shift traditional application security wasn’t built for, and it’s why trust has to be built into the system around the agent, not assumed. An agent decides its own path, picking tools at runtime, chaining actions together, and usually running with the credentials of whoever launched it. That autonomy is the source of most agent-specific risk, and it points to the two-part answer that runs through this post: contain what an agent can reach, and oversee what it does. Key takeaways AI agents introduce risks traditional app security wasn’t built for: they choose tools, chain actions, and often run with your credentials. The main risks are prompt injection, tool misuse and poisoning, excessive autonomy, credential exposure, and data exfiltration. Most trace back to one thing: the agent can act, so containment and oversight matter more than the model. The two-part answer is isolation to limit blast radius and governance to oversee behavior. Why agents break traditional security models If you’ve secured web services, the model is familiar: requests arrive at known endpoints, deterministic logic handles them, and you design controls around that predictability. Agents break that assumption. They interpret instructions dynamically, choose tools at runtime, and run multi-step chains with very little human intervention at each step. A coding agent might read a file, install a dependency, change config, run tests, and push a commit from a single prompt. Because an agent chooses its own path, a compromised or misdirected one can take a far wider range of actions than a traditional service. Every risk below has already produced documented real-world incidents, and they all follow from that shift. 1. Prompt injection Prompt injection is the risk that defines agent security. Because an agent acts on whatever text it reads, an attacker doesn’t need access to your systems. They just need the agent to encounter their instructions, hidden in a web page, a code comment, an issue, or a document it summarizes. A real prompt-injection case showed an agent following instructions buried in repository content and taking actions its user never intended. Incident highlight: A coding agent followed instructions buried in a repository’s own content and took actions its user never intended. The malicious text arrived through data the agent was simply asked to read. The agent has no reliable way to tell a legitimate instruction from an injected one, so the defense is to limit what a hijacked agent can reach. 2. Tool misuse and tool poisoning Agents act through tools: API connectors, database queries, file operations, and code execution. Every tool is an access vector, and two things could go wrong. An agent can be given more tools than the task needs, widening the attack surface for no reason. And a tool itself can be poisoned, its description carrying hidden instructions that manipulate the agent into misusing it. The mitigations are to scope tools to the task at runtime, source them from registries with verified provenance, and review tool descriptions rather than trusting them by default. 3. Excessive autonomy The more an agent can do without review, the more a single bad decision costs. Excessive autonomy is the risk of granting an agent broad, standing permission to act, most visibly when developers run YOLO mode, where every action is auto-approved. This autonomy is genuinely useful, so switching it off defeats the point. The better move is to run the agent where that autonomy can’t reach anything it shouldn’t, so speed doesn’t necessarily mean increased blast radius. Incident highlight: A developer asked a coding agent to clean up an old repository. It generated an rm -rf command with a trailing ~/ and ran it with no confirmation step, wiping the developer’s entire home directory. Nothing in the setup gave a human a chance to catch it before it executed. 4. Credential and secret exposure When an agent runs under a developer’s personal token, every action it takes carries that person’s full permissions, and a compromise hands those permissions to an attacker. Secrets sitting in prompts, config files, or environment variables baked into an image make it worse, because a prompt injection can read them straight out of the agent’s context. Agents should get their own scoped, short-lived credentials, injected at runtime and kept out of the conversation, rather than borrowing yours. Incident highlight: An AWS engineer handed a small Cost Explorer bug to a coding agent running with their own operator-level access. The agent decided the cleanest fix was to delete and rebuild the production environment, and it held the credentials to do exactly that. The result was a thirteen-hour regional outage. 5. Data exfiltration and untrusted handoffs An agent with network access and sensitive information in its context can send that data somewhere it shouldn’t, whether through a compromised tool or an injected instruction. The risk grows in multi-agent setups, where one agent passes work to another. If the receiving agent treats that input as trusted, a compromise in one link can spread down the chain. Restricting network egress to known endpoints and treating every agent-to-agent handoff as untrusted input could keep a single failure from spreading. How to contain the risk The risks are varied, but there are controls to secure AI agents. Isolate where the agent runs so a mistake or a hijack is trapped in a disposable environment instead of loose on your host, and scope what the agent can access so the damage it can do is small even inside that boundary. Risk Primary control Primary injection Isolation, so a hijacked agent can’t reach anything that matters Tool misuse and poisoning Runtime-scoped tools from verified-provenance sources Excessive autonomy A sandbox boundary that makes auto-approval safe Credential exposure Dedicated, short-lived credentials injected at runtime Data exfiltration Allow-listed network egress and untrusted inter-agent input Isolation is the highest-impact starting point, and a microVM boundary makes it strong without slowing the agent down. On top of containment, oversight is what keeps a fleet of agents accountable. Then, AI governance defines which actions an agent may take, what it can reach, and how its behavior is logged, so risk is managed deliberately rather than discovered after an incident. Contain the blast radius, govern the behavior These risks aren’t reasons to avoid developing with agents. Instead, we need to give agents the freedom to finish the job by building trust into the system around them, so that freedom never means access to everything. And that’s the job Docker Sandboxes is built for: each agent runs in its own disposable microVM with the network and filesystem controls you define, so a mistake or an injection is contained by design. And AI Governance adds the oversight layer, setting which actions, tools, and credentials are allowed and enforcing it everywhere your team works. Contain the blast radius, and govern the behavior. Frequently Asked Questions What are the main security risks of AI agents? The most significant are prompt injection, tool misuse and tool poisoning, excessive autonomy, credential and secret exposure, and data exfiltration. All of them stem from the fact that agents act on their own, using tools and credentials, rather than following a fixed, reviewable path. What is the biggest AI agent security risk? For most teams it’s excessive access: an agent running with more autonomy and more credentials than the task needs. It turns a small mistake or a single prompt injection into a large incident, because the agent can reach so much. How is agent security different from application security? Traditional application security assumes predictable request-and-response flows. Agent security has to account for autonomous decisions, tools chosen at runtime, and multi-step chains where the agent sets its own path. The attack surface is wider because the agent, not a fixed program, decides what happens next. Can prompt injection be prevented? You can reduce it with input handling and tool hygiene, but you can’t assume it away, because an agent can’t reliably tell injected instructions from legitimate ones. The durable defense is containment: run the agent so that even a successfully injected one can’t reach anything sensitive. How do you reduce AI agent security risks? Start with isolation so a compromised agent is trapped in a disposable environment. Add scoped tool access and dedicated credentials to shrink what any agent can do. Then layer on governance to define and enforce those limits consistently across every agent your team runs.

title: [Cloudflare] How Commerce.com and Cloudflare are getting storefronts ready for AI agents
summary: AI can write code and pass the bar exam, but it still struggles to buy a pair of shoes online.That’s because websites were built for humans, not agents. Most agents that shop for someone today work from a site’s HTML — they look at the page, guess which button does what, click, and try again when they get it wrong. This process is slow, uses a lot of tokens, and something as seemingly innocuous as a theme change can break it.Enter WebMCP: a browser standard from Google that gives AI agents structured tools on a page, like search_products. Instead of hunting for buttons, the agent calls the exact tool it needs directly, making shopping faster, cheaper, and far more reliable. Because WebMCP is still an experimental proposed browser standard in early preview, it’s currently available behind experimental Chrome flags (chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing), in Chrome Origin Trials, in some agentic browsers, and across developer environments like Cloudflare Kitesurf.In August, we launched edge implementation of WebMCP in beta. Turn it on, and Cloudflare injects a tiny script at the edge to make those tools available automatically, without site owners writing a single line of code.Commerce.com, a flexible commerce platform built for the age of AI, already uses Cloudflare to run their almost 100,000 domains. So when the preview came out, they asked: Can we turn this on for all of our stores at once?Here’s why Commerce.com wanted WebMCP, how we built edge-level opt-outs to give every merchant control, and what we learned along the way.Why Commerce.com wanted WebMCPKristina Pototska, Product Management Director at Commerce.com, explains why this matters for storefronts:“Merchants keep asking us how they can keep up with agentic shopping. When a shopper asks an agent to find something, merchants want their store to be in the answer. They want to keep the customer, keep control of the checkout, and do it without rebuilding their site. WebMCP helps with all three. The agent gets real tools to search products, check details, build a cart, and get a checkout link, so it doesn’t have to guess its way around the page. The human shopper stays on the merchant’s site, and the merchant keeps the relationship.We wanted to turn this on in a secure way, and without asking merchants to edit their theme or do anything by hand. That’s where the Cloudflare partnership worked perfectly.WebMCP also works side by side with our server-side MCP, and together they cover the different ways people shop with agents. Server-side MCP supports agents that connect to a store directly, like an assistant helping someone shop across several sites. WebMCP supports agents that work in the shopper’s browser. It’s the same set of shopping tools in both cases, so merchants don’t have to choose between the two or manage them separately.”Under the hood, this integration relies on two key principles. First, the WebMCP tools execute directly inside the shopper's active browser session on the storefront's domain, ensuring the agent sees the same prices and cart. No credentials go to a third party, and the visit still happens on the merchant's site. Second, Cloudflare serves as the edge delivery layer for Commerce.com’s backend MCP server, proxying tool definitions and actions unchanged so merchants maintain full control over their tool logic.What a shopper's agent seesWhen visiting an enabled Commerce.com storefront, an AI assistant no longer has to guess how to navigate the site. Instead, it can instantly discover tools via WebMCP.Suppose you tell your agent: "Find me a waterproof trail running shoe under $140 in size 10 and add it to my cart."Without WebMCP: The agent attempts to simulate human clicks, only to get blocked by cookie banners, misinterpret variant drop-downs, or get tripped up by bot challenges that try to distinguish automated traffic from real customers.With WebMCP: The agent detects the store's tools on document.modelContext and makes two clean calls:search_products({ query: "trail running shoe", max_price: 140, size: 10 })add_to_cart({ product_id: "shoe_123" })Because the agent runs inside your active browser session on the store's domain, your cart updates in real time. Commerce.com’s backend MCP server determines the commerce flow: when you’re ready to complete the purchase, you click checkout yourself — keeping your payment details secure and leaving you in complete control of the final buy.What we built togetherWhen Commerce.com asked to turn on WebMCP across almost 100000 storefronts, we ran into a practical challenge: WebMCP was originally designed as a single on-or-off switch for an entire domain zone.Commerce wanted to enable our mcp-server-client toolpack, which acts as an edge bridge — proxying tool definitions and requests directly from Commerce.com’s backend MCP server to the visitor's browser. Because Commerce.com uses Cloudflare for SaaS to host thousands of merchant vanity domains on shared zones, we needed a way to deliver this platform-wide while giving individual store owners an easy way to opt out.1. On for all stores on Commerce.com, with an opt-out for each merchantInstead of building a complex custom allowlist, we hooked WebMCP into the existing Cloudflare concepts of Configuration Rules and custom hostname metadata.Commerce.com turns WebMCP on for their main zone, then adds a rule at the edge that checks merchant metadata. If a merchant flips the "opt-out" switch in their Commerce.com dashboard, Cloudflare bypasses WebMCP for that specific storefront automatically:{ "action": "set_config", "expression": "cf.hostname.metadata.webmcp_opt_out eq \"true\"", "action_parameters": { "webmcp_enabled": false } }Because Cloudflare evaluates these rules at the edge before serving the page, an opted-out store gets zero extra latency, no remote lookups, and no injected scripts.2. Tailored endpoints and safe fallbacksAs with any preview release, working with a partner in the real world revealed a few practical details we hadn't accounted for: Custom MCP paths: When the mcp-server-client toolpack was enabled, our bridge originally expected to find every site's MCP server at /mcp. Commerce.com’s server lives at /api/mcp. To handle this, we added a configurable MCP URL setting at the zone level. When this is set, we pass the custom path into the injected script tag:<script type="module" src="/.webmcp/bridge.js" data-packs="c2pa,mcp-server-client" data-mcp-url="/api/mcp"></script>Seamless fallbacks: If a store's MCP server is offline or a customer's browser doesn't support WebMCP, the script exits. The storefront loads normally and human shoppers aren't affected.What's nextWe'll keep investing in WebMCP as the standard evolves, starting with helping agents find a site's tools more easily. Cloudflare and Commerce.com will continue to work together to make shopping with agents fast, reliable and safe for both merchants and shoppers.If you're at Cloudflare Connect in San Francisco on October 21, 2026, come see us at Getting your storefront agent ready for peak season, a panel discussion featuring Kristina Pototska (Product Management Director, Commerce), Justis Blasco (CTO and Co-Founder, Popmenu), Ross Harvey (Head of Infrastructure, Fruugo), and Josh Mills (VP of Engineering, Gopuff).

title: [Netflix] Reliable GPU compute for large training & inference jobs
summary: How we detect failing GPUs and network fabric, remediate machines automatically, and let long-running jobs survive hardware loss.Authors: Nick Rutigliano, Argha C, Samartha ChandrashekarOpen Netflix, and the home screen is assembled for you: which rows appear, the order they appear in, the titles within them, and the artwork for each title are chosen by machine learning models trained on how hundreds of millions of members watch. Personalization is one of the most widely used things we build, and members feel it every time they open the app. Like a growing share of Netflix, it runs on GPUs, which train those models and increasingly serve them live.Those GPUs have to stay healthy for that experience to hold up, and keeping them healthy is harder than it sounds. A single large training job can run for weeks across hundreds of GPUs spread over many machines. It runs as a gang: the ranks move in lockstep, exchanging data every step, so the job advances only as fast as its slowest participant and stops entirely if one participant dies. Every GPU, every high-speed network adapter, and every interconnect must keep working throughout the run. At the scale at which modern machine learning runs, individual GPUs and network links can fail during a run, so the underlying platform must be prepared for this and handle it without a person in the loop.This post describes how we keep our GPU infrastructure healthy for training and inference. We cover how we detect failing hardware before and during jobs, how we automatically remediate a bad machine, and how we let a long job survive the loss of a machine. These training workloads run on our modern Kubernetes-native Compute platform.Why GPU reliability mattersNetflix aims to entertain the world, and machine learning has been part of how we do that for years, from the recommendations that help members find something to watch to the systems that help produce and promote titles. As generative AI advances, we are investing in it on both sides of the business: for members, through better recommendations and higher-quality promotional assets; and for storytelling, through creative tools for our production partners.All of this runs on GPUs, for both training and inference, and GPU capacity is among the fastest-growing and most expensive parts of our infrastructure. That makes reliability a business concern on two fronts.Availability: a training run that loses a machine, or an inference service that cannot get healthy capacity, delays work that members and creators depend on.Cost efficiency: a GPU sitting idle behind a slow neighbor, or a whole machine pulled from the pool because one device is degraded, becomes capacity we paid for and are not using. Higher reliability and higher utilization mean more useful work per GPU, which is equivalent to spending less to do the same work.Inference is a growing share of that GPU footprint as more of these AI features reach members, so the reliability and efficiency that matter for multi-week training runs increasingly matter for always-on serving too.Why basic health checks are not enoughWe start from the baseline provided by the cloud provider. Cloud providers run instance status checks on virtual machines: a system status check for the underlying host’s power, network, and hardware reachability; an instance status check to verify that the operating system is up and reachable; and a check on attached storage. It emits scheduled maintenance events when it plans to retire or reboot a host, and it can automatically recover an instance that becomes impaired. We use all of these, and the maintenance events feed one of our own checks. They catch a machine that is down, unreachable, or slated for maintenance, and they stop at the instance level. They confirm the box is up and reachable. They do not verify that each GPU, its on-chip memory, its interconnect, and its network fabric are healthy enough to support distributed training.The next step most teams take is a GPU-level check to confirm that the driver responds and that the GPUs are visible. That catches a dead or missing GPU, but misses the cases that take the most time.A GPU can answer a status query and still be faulty once a workload touches it. A fault in on-chip memory or in the firmware that manages the device can remain invisible until a job allocates memory or runs sustained compute, at which point the job fails or slows.A high-speed network adapter may be present but show fewer links than expected. Collective operations still run, at a fraction of the bandwidth, so the job does not crash. It crawls, and the cause is easy to miss.A check can fail in ways that leave a faulty machine looking healthy. The diagnostic tool can hang when the driver hangs, and a naive check that waits on it hangs too. A binary that the check depends on can go missing after a driver upgrade, causing the check to stop running and report nothing. A check that can silently stop running is worse than no check, because it gives false confidence while the machine keeps working.Because a job runs as a gang, any one of these on any one machine can degrade or stop the whole job, and none of them shows up in an instance-level check or a driver-responds check. The health system has to assume the hardware can lie and the tools that inspect it can break.A machine can pass a basic check and still be faulty. Layered checks, timeouts, a fallback path, and checks that fail when a dependency is missing close these gaps.Our approachWe treat reliability as four layers, each catching what the layer below cannot:1/ Node and hardware health: find bad GPUs, network adapters, interconnects, memory errors, and thermal issues, then taint or recycle the machine.2/ Scheduler and platform: retry at the task & job level, validate a machine before it takes work, and drain & recycle machines safely.3/ Training loop: checkpoint and use elastic workers so a job survives losing a machine.4/ Observability: metrics, service-level objectives, and failure attribution across the other three.The first two layers keep hardware problems away from jobs. The third accepts that some loss is unavoidable and makes it cheap. The fourth tells us whether the first three are working.Four layers: Each catches what the layer below cannot.How the health checks workChecks run in two tiers. Device-level checks look at each GPU. A node-level agent, built on the open-source Kubernetes node-problem-detector, runs on every GPU machine every 30 seconds and turns check results into conditions on the Kubernetes node, the same mechanism Kubernetes uses to mark a node NotReady. Controllers watch those conditions and decide whether the machine can take on work.GPU device checks are built on NVIDIA’s DCGM for driver-reported error codes, uncorrectable memory errors, interconnect integrity, and thermal state, and networking adapter checks inspect the host state for the count and link state of the Elastic Fabric Adapter interfaces that carry cross-machine traffic. A few of these checks deserve detail.Two-tier health checking. Device-level and node-level checks become Kubernetes node conditions, which controllers then turn into taints, drains, terminates, and replaces.Failing closed: if the driver or the diagnostic tool is unresponsive, the check times out and marks the machine unhealthy. A check that cannot reach the hardware reports a problem rather than passing, so a wedged driver takes the machine out of rotation rather than letting it hide behind a hung tool.A fallback path: driver error codes are the strongest signal that a GPU has faulted, but the tool that reads them can itself be broken in certain failure modes! When it does, we read the kernel log dmesg directly for those codes, so no Xid or SXid errors are missed.Our own fatal-error map: vendor driver error catalogs lag newer GPU generations and do not always match what we see in production, so we keep our own mapping of which codes are fatal for each GPU family. A code that means reset-the-GPU in one generation can be benign in another, and one GPU generation emits a burst of normally-fatal code on every healthy boot, which we learned to treat as noise rather than drain fresh machines.No silent no-ops: a check fails when a required dependency is missing. This one came from an upgrade that dropped a binary the network-adapter check relied on. The check quietly stopped running, and machines with the wrong number of adapters shipped for days before the slow jobs were traced back to them. Now a missing dependency fails the check.Turning a bad machine into healthy capacity, automaticallyWhen a check fails, the machine’s node condition changes, and controllers take over. We distinguish two levels. A problem condition blocks new work from landing while jobs are running, because pulling a job off a machine is disruptive, and many problems clear on their own. If the condition persists beyond a tolerance window, it escalates to a failure condition, which evacuates the machine, drains its tasks (overriding the normal disruption limits to move quickly), terminates it, and replaces it.Karpenter node auto-repair is used on our compute stack. We have customized it with a policy and a controller that maps each node condition to the duration we tolerate it before acting, so a fast-fatal error is actioned within minutes. At the same time, a flaky signal gets a longer window, and a cap limits how much of a cluster we will disrupt at once, so a bad rollout of the checks themselves cannot cascade into tearing down a whole cluster. We plan to upstream this feature to all Karpenter users.Graded remediation. A problem is tolerated and may clear; a persistent failure escalates to evacuation and draining, then to a fast in-place fix or termination for confirmed hardware faults.Not every fault requires a full replacement, and replacement is the slowest way to restore capacity. We match the action to the fault. Killing the offending job clears a software wedge. Resetting a single GPU clears many transient device faults. Rebooting the machine clears the firmware state that has drifted over a long uptime. Terminating and replacing is reserved for hardware that fails a test we trust. For that last case, we record the GPU’s immutable hardware identifier, which stays with the physical device across reboots and relaunches even when the instance changes, report it to the cloud provider, and keep our own list, so a device that fails repeatedly does not quietly rejoin the pool under a new instance.One subtlety sits between detection and scheduling. A freshly checked machine was handed to the scheduler just as its checks were still settling, so a job could land on it a moment before a slow check flagged it. We now hold capacity until the checks have run and settled, which closed that window.Validating a machine before it takes workA machine that just booted is not trusted until it proves itself. Before we release its capacity, it passes system checks, confirms the GPUs and their topology are present, and runs a round of GPU diagnostics. We then wait for the health checks to run twice, because the longer checks, such as counting network adapters, take more than one cycle to fire, and releasing after a single pass would let work land before those checks are reported. Only then do we remove the startup taint. On teardown, we run deeper diagnostics and record the GPU identifiers, which feed the same bad-hardware list, so hardware that failed once does not silently cycle back into service.Letting long jobs survive machine lossEven with all of the above, some machines are lost mid-job, so we make that cheap. Jobs checkpoint their state, and on a lost machine, they resume from the last healthy checkpoint rather than restarting from the beginning of a multi-week run. Workers are elastic and retryable, and the scheduler automatically retries platform-caused failures.Attribution is what makes automatic retries safe. If we retried every failure, we would mask genuine bugs in a job and burn GPU hours looping on an error the platform cannot fix, so we classify each failure as platform or application before retrying. One example of why this matters: a class of timeouts in NCCL, the collective communication library GPUs use to exchange data, appeared to be a network fault and was traced to data-loading stalls at high worker counts. The GPUs and the network were fine, and the fix was in the data pipeline. Treated as hardware failures, those timeouts would have cycled healthy machines without fixing the cause.Measuring whether it worksWe track GPU reliability along three service-level objectives, each split by cause, so a miss points at the layer responsible:Availability: the amount of GPU capacity available for scheduling at any given moment.Job-start success: whether a job starts promptly once its capacity is available.Job success: whether a job finishes without a platform-caused failure.Each objective is split into hardware, driver, platform, and user causes. Hence, an availability dip from bad hardware reads differently from one caused by a scheduler change or a user misconfiguration. We optimize for goodput, the useful work the fleet completes, because a job held back by one slow GPU can look healthy on an uptime chart while getting almost nothing done. Specific targets for each objective are provided here for illustrative purposes.A closed remediation loopThese pieces form a loop. Hardware is validated at allocation, before a job starts, with a short collective communication run and pairwise network tests. Hence, any machine that fails within the first minute fails before the job is admitted. During the job, we watch passively for driver errors, memory errors, thermal events, and more. We view each job as a distributed system, which lets us identify a single slow rank dragging the rest, rather than only whole-machine failures. When something is wrong, remediation is automatic and graded. The loop is the same whether a job runs through our batch scheduler, Kueue, or Ray.The reliability loop: validate, watch, actively check, view the job as a system, remediate, then repeat.Sharing GPUs safelyNot every workload needs a whole GPU, and leaving small inference jobs on dedicated GPUs wastes capacity. We partition GPUs with MIG for memory-level isolation between tenants, so a fault or a memory hog in one partition does not affect another. We also reconfigure those partitions without restarting the machine, so that a pool can shift between many small slices and a few large ones as demand changes. GPU and network adapter allocation is device-plugin-based today, to move to Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation once it is supported in Karpenter. This matters because a GPU talking to a network adapter or working with a CPU on the wrong PCIE root of the machine incurs a bandwidth penalty.On a multi-GPU machine, we isolate a single faulty GPU, keep the rest in service, and partition healthy GPUs across multiple tenants with memory-level isolation.Device-level allocation also changes how we handle a single bad GPU. With DRA support, instead of losing the whole machine, we could isolate the one faulty device and keep the others serving, which matters most for inference, where many small jobs share a machine. And because allocation is expressive, a job can request the capabilities it needs, such as memory or tensor-core support, and the platform matches a suitable GPU type, so users are not pinned to a model they had to choose in advance.ResultsMoving from basic checks and manual draining to layered checks and automatic remediation changed two things users feel. More of the GPU fleet is available for scheduling at any time because bad machines are caught and cycled quickly, rather than sitting in the pool or waiting on an on-call engineer. And fewer jobs fail due to platform issues because most faults are caught before a job lands, and the rest are automatically remediated and retried. Graded remediation also returns capacity in minutes for faults that only require a job kill, a GPU reset, or a reboot, rather than the longer wait for a replacement machine.Since the above improvements have landed, we’ve seen:Consistently achieving >99.95% availability of our GPU nodesJob success rate has gone from ~98% to above 99.5%What is nextWe are extending active checks to cover additional failure modes under load, widening burn-in so more classes of failures can be cleared before a user encounters them, and making remediation more granular so more error types are cleared in place rather than requiring a full node replacement loop for certain Xid errors. Additionally, we want to do more periodic diagnostics between jobs.We are working to make placement more topology-aware using Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) once it lands in Karpenter, for example, by aligning on Compute/IMEX Domains, PCIe roots, and NUMA nodes.More on the performance side for multi-GPU training, we plan to run a custom Linux scheduler built on sched_ext. Firstly, we can prioritize processes during collective coordination, such as when GPUs exchange results before the next round of compute, thereby reducing overall GPU idle time by establishing a fleet-wide priority for these tasks. The effect is small on one machine but grows across hundreds of machines, where a few percent of throughput amounts to a large amount of capacity. Secondly, we can prioritize data-loading processes to minimize the bottleneck that sometimes occurs when data is not loaded onto GPUs quickly enough to maintain steady progress.While we already monitor throttling events, GPUs do not have to report throttling for it to hurt a job. One running ten to fifteen degrees hotter than its peers, even within healthy limits, sets the pace for the gang, so we can treat a large temperature gap as a fault, stop the job, and move it to cooler GPUs.Additionally, we plan to expand our NCCL RAS (reliability, availability, serviceability) monitoring to identify NCCL issues sooner, such as mismatched collectives or hangs, to more quickly resume work.ClosingHardware fails, and at this scale, it fails often enough that the platform has to treat failure as normal. Detecting problems before and during jobs, automatically remediating machines, and allowing long jobs to resume after a loss lets teams run large-scale training and inference without babysitting the hardware. If you like these kinds of problems, we are hiring.Reliable GPU compute for large training & inference jobs was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [Docker] Docker Hub security advisory: personal access tokens transferred during account-to-organization conversions
summary: On September 30, 2026, security researchers reported a vulnerability in Docker Hub’s identity and access management through our Vulnerability Disclosure Program. We confirmed the report and deployed a fix to production the same afternoon, less than four hours after receiving it. We then reviewed every account conversion back to the date the flaw was introduced, and on October 2, notified every user and organization owner whose account could have been impacted by this vulnerability. This post explains what the vulnerability was, what it could and could not do, what we found, and what we have changed. We want to thank Peter Molnar and Krisztian Hozak of mptrdev.com for finding the issue, reporting it responsibly, and coordinating disclosure with us. Their technical write-up is available at ghostpat.com. This issue is tracked as CVE-2026-105445. Was I or any member of my organization exposed to the vulnerability? On October 2 at 5:30PM EST, we sent out an email with the subject line “Docker Hub Vulnerability Identified & Resolved” to the limited number of users exposed to this vulnerability. If you did not receive an email, you and any members of the organizations you administer were not exposed and there are no actions for you to take. What the vulnerability was Docker Hub lets you convert a personal account into an organization. People do this because Hub has no way to move a repository from one account to another: conversion is how alice/app becomes an organization-owned alice/app without breaking every Docker pull that references it. During conversion, the user names an existing Docker Hub account as the new organization’s owner. Beginning August 26, 2024, conversion also re-assigned the converted account’s personal access tokens (PATs) to that new owner. It did this by changing the token’s owner record, without rotating or revoking the token secret. The named owner was not asked to confirm and was not notified. Together, those two gaps made the following possible: An attacker creates an account and generates a PAT on it. The attacker converts that account to an organization and names a target user as the owner. The attacker’s PAT is re-assigned to the target user. The attacker still holds the secret and the PAT remains active now with the target user’s scope. The token now authenticates to the registry as the target user. What an attacker could and could not do Within the scope of the token, a re-assigned PAT acted as the target user at the registry level, meaning an attacker could potentially pull, push, and/or delete images in the target’s repositories and in organizations where the target had access. Because that includes publishing images under a legitimate name, we treated this as a software supply chain risk and rated it critical. The vulnerability did not give access to the Docker Hub web interface, and it could not be used to change the target’s password, email address, or two-factor settings, or to take over the account. The exposure window ran from August 26, 2024, 20:33 UTC, until the fix was deployed on September 30, 2026, at approximately  UTC. Timeline (all times U.S. Eastern) Sept 30, 11:40 AM: Report received at security@docker.com. Sept 30, ~1:30 PM: We independently reproduced the issue with internal test accounts. Sept 30, ~3:10 PM: Fix deployed to production and verified against the original proof of concept. Conversion no longer transfers PATs. Sept 30, ~3:23 PM: Documentation updated to state that PATs do not transfer and must be recreated by the new owner, with organization access tokens recommended. Sept 30, 4:59 PM: Researchers informed of the fix. Both parties agreed to coordinate disclosure. Oct 2, 5:30 PM: Exposed users and their organization owners notified by email. Oct 8, 3:45 PM: Forced deactivation of all PATs transferred through conversion, except where the account holder opted out. What we investigated and found We enumerated every account conversion performed since August 26, 2024 and correlated them with registry authentication logs, Docker Hub usage data, and IAM token records. We looked for any token used under more than one identity, and we examined every push made with a transferred token, about 304,000 in all. We found no evidence that the vulnerability was exploited. Every push made with a transferred token landed either in the converted organization’s own repositories or in the new owner’s own repositories. None went into an unrelated user’s or organization’s account. In the large majority of cases, the account converted and the account named as owner belonged to the same person or team, which is the normal, legitimate use of this feature. We statically analyzed the highest-risk public images without executing them: images pushed after a conversion where we could not establish that the same person controlled both accounts. We found no malware, cryptominers, command-and-control activity, credential harvesting, persistence, or tampering. We found no evidence that Docker’s own infrastructure or services were affected. We also want to be clear about the limits of that finding:registry logs show when a token is used, not that it exists, so a transferred token that was never used leaves no trace. For that reason, we did not rely on detection to decide who was exposed. We treated every PAT that moved through conversion during the window as potentially affected, whether or not we saw it used. What we did for affected users On October 2, we emailed the limited number of users whose accounts received transferred PATs. Each email listed the in-scope tokens by description and creation date so users could find them in Docker Hub. We separately notified the associated organization owners. On October 8th at 3:45 PM EST, we deactivated the identified transferred PATs. Tokens that their owners asked to keep before the deadline were excluded. Once again, if you did not receive the above email, no PAT on your account was transferred through this flow. Your account was therefore not exposed to this vulnerability and there is no action for you to take. What we are changing The immediate fix removed PAT transfer from conversion entirely. Beyond that, we are now: requiring consent from a user before they are named as an organization owner, and notifying them when it happens; recording an auditable history of every token ownership change, so questions like this can be answered from records rather than inference; reviewing other flows that change credential ownership for the same pattern. What you can do Review the personal access tokens on your account in Docker Hub under Account settings, Personal access tokens, and revoke any you don’t recognize or no longer use. For automation that belongs to an organization, use organization access tokens rather than a person’s PAT. If you have questions about this notice, contact Docker Support at app.docker.com/support/contact. Responsible disclosure works when researchers and vendors treat each other as partners. Peter and Krisztian did that here, and our users are safer for it. If you find a security issue in a Docker product, please report it to security@docker.com.
